Uniqueness of the Higgs.

On the genus-4 Bring's surface, the Seifert surface of T(2,8) has genus 3, filling 3 of the 4 available handles. Up to isotopy, there is exactly one way to embed a genus-3 surface into a genus-4 surface leaving one handle free. The next link T(2,10) would require genus 4 (all handles), saturating the surface and precluding the coexistence of Borromean and knot structures. Therefore, T(2,8) is the unique Higgs candidate.
prop:s5-equivariant-torus-knots:
Proposition S_5-equivariant torus-knot embeddings: the \mathbb{Z}_s and monodromy tests. Let \Sigma be a Riemann surface with automorphism group \mathrm{Aut}(\Sigma) = S_5 (Bring's surface). A torus knot T_{2, s} with s \geq 3 coprime to 2 admits an equivariant embedding into \Sigma if and only if

  s  \in  \{3,\, 5\}.

An equivariant embedding preserves the intrinsic cyclic symmetry \mathbb{Z}_s of the knot.

Two tests. The fibration of T_{2,s} has monodromy of order 2s. For odd s the monodromy group is \mathbb{Z}_{2s} \cong \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_s, the two rotations of the torus knot taken together. The criterion above is the \mathbb{Z}_s test: it asks only that the \mathbb{Z}_s rotation be realised in S_5. The stronger monodromy test asks that the whole \mathbb{Z}_{2s} be realised, that is, that S_5 contain an element of order 2s. This holds if and only if

  s = 3.

Under the monodromy test only T_{2,3} passes; T_{2,5} fails because S_5 has no element of order 10. The \mathbb{Z}_s test is the weaker of the two, and a statement that a knot is S_5-equivariant should say which test it uses.

prf:s5-equivariant-torus-knots:
Proof Proof of s5 equivariant torus knots. An equivariant embedding requires \mathbb{Z}_s \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Aut}(\Sigma) = S_5. The cyclic symmetry of the knot must match a symmetry of the ambient surface. An injection \mathbb{Z}_s \hookrightarrow S_5 exists if and only if S_5 contains an element of order s. The orders of elements in S_5 are the least common multiples of the parts of integer partitions of 5.

See Table.

The realised orders in S_5 are \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}. The condition \gcd(2, s) = 1 forces odd s \geq 3. This restricts the possible orders to \{3, 5\}. \square

The monodromy test. An element of order 2s with s odd and s \geq 3 must have order 6, 10 or 30 among the divisors of 60. An element whose order is divisible by 5 is a 5-cycle, of order exactly 5, so orders 10 and 30 do not occur. Order 6 is realised by a transposition times a disjoint 3-cycle. Hence the monodromy test holds only for s = 3. \square

Corollary. Among torus knots T_{2, s} with s \geq 3, exactly two admit cyclic-symmetry-preserving embeddings into \Sigma_4 (Bring's surface): T_{2, 3} and T_{2, 5}. Any other torus knot of this family either breaks the symmetry in the embedding or fails to embed topologically (Seifert genus > 4, or s \geq 11).

Comparison with genus-based embedding. Pure topological (Seifert-genus) embedding into \Sigma_4 admits four knots: T_{2, 3}, T_{2, 5}, T_{2, 7}, and T_{2, 9}. The stronger equivariant criterion retains only T_{2, 3} and T_{2, 5}. The knots T_{2, 7} and T_{2, 9} are topologically admissible but symmetry-broken.
rem:symmetry-preserving-leptons:
Remark Symmetry-preserving versus symmetry-broken lepton generators. The classification of prop:s5-equivariant-torus-knots admits a sharp physical reading. The three charged lepton generations map to torus knots:

  \text{electron} \;=\; T_{2,3},
  \qquad
  \text{muon} \;=\; T_{2,5},
  \qquad
  \text{tau} \;=\; T_{2,7}.

Under pure topological embedding (Seifert genus \leq 4), all three fit on Bring's surface. Under the stronger equivariant criterion—preserving the knot's intrinsic cyclic symmetry along the embedding—the proposition cuts the list to two:

Particle Knot Cyclic symmetry \mathbb{Z}_s \hookrightarrow S_5? Embedding
electron T_{2,3} \mathbb{Z}_3 yes (3-cycle) symmetry-preserving
muon T_{2,5} \mathbb{Z}_5 yes (5-cycle) symmetry-preserving
tau T_{2,7} \mathbb{Z}_7 no (no order-7 element in S_5) symmetry-broken
(ghost) T_{2,9} \mathbb{Z}_9 no (no order-9 element) symmetry-broken, saturates g=4
(ghost) T_{2,11} \mathbb{Z}_{11} no doubly excluded (g = 5 > 4)

Reading. The electron and muon are the only leptons whose cyclic rotational symmetry is realized by a genuine element of \mathrm{Aut}(\Sigma_4) = S_5. The tau embeds topologically by virtue of its genus (g(T_{2,7}) = 3 \leq 4) but fails equivariance: its \mathbb{Z}_7 symmetry is not a subgroup of S_5. The tau is a lepton in the topological spectrum, but not in the symmetry spectrum.

Physical consequence. If lepton-generation structure derives from the cyclic symmetry of a \Sigma_4-embedded torus knot, the equivariant criterion predicts exactly two generations of charged leptons. Three generations are observed, matching the topological-embedding criterion. The equivariant proposition sharpens this: tau carries its mass because the symmetry-broken embedding still admits a Seifert surface, not because an S_5-compatible cyclic structure exists. This aligns with the weight-identification picture (rem:weight-identification-consequences), where the electron and muon representations fit into the \mathbb{Z}_5-graded structure of the \mathcal{X}_5 aether.

Scope. The proposition does not prohibit the tau. It dictates that the tau requires a different mechanism (symmetry-broken embedding) than the electron and muon (symmetry-preserving embedding). The genus saturation at T_{2,9} excludes fourth and higher generations. The three-generation structure is 2 + 1, not 3 + 0.
